theme: May God be gracious, all the nations praise him
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 67. It is a short prayer that God would bless his people so that all nations would know and praise him. It reads like the first missionary journey of Acts 13 turned into song.
settingTheScene: Psalm 67 begins with the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 (“the LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you”), but turns it outward. The blessing is not an end in itself. Israel is blessed so that the nations may be blessed. That is the Abrahamic promise at work, which is the reason why Acts 13 quotes Isaiah 49:6. Reading it as Paul and Barnabas set out on their journey makes the missions theme clear.
observation: “May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us” (v. 1).
“That your way may be known on earth” (v. 2).
“Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!” (v. 3).
“Let the nations be glad and sing for joy” (v. 4).
“For you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth” (v. 4).
“The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, has blessed us” (v. 6).
“God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!” (v. 7).
interpretation:
The psalm starts with a prayer for blessing: “May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us.” This is borrowed from the benediction that Aaron and his sons spoke over Israel. But the next word is “that.” The blessing has a purpose: “that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.” Israel asks for God’s favor, not for its own sake, but so that the whole world may see and know the LORD.

The refrain follows: “Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!” It appears twice, in verses 3 and 5, as the center of the psalm. The goal of all God’s work is that the nations praise him. In between, the psalm says why the nations can be glad: God judges the peoples with equity and guides the nations upon earth. His rule is just and good. The nations are not simply objects of judgment but people whom God guides. This is a vision of a world finally under the good rule of the true God.

Then the psalm returns to blessing: “The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, has blessed us. God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!” The harvest is the sign of God’s blessing, and it becomes a motive for missions. The psalm ends with the whole world fearing the LORD.

This is the pattern of the Abrahamic covenant: “I will bless you… so that you will be a blessing… and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” It is the pattern of Acts: the apostles are sent to the nations. And it is the church’s prayer today. We pray for God to bless us, not for comfort alone, but so that we can be used to bless others and bring praise to his name. The final picture, in Revelation 7:9, is of people from every nation, tribe, people, and language praising God. Psalm 67 is the prayer that leads there.
connection: Numbers 6:22-27 is the priestly blessing. Genesis 12:1-3 is the Abrahamic promise. Isaiah 49:6 and 2:2-4 speak of the nations coming to the LORD. Psalm 117 and 96 also call the nations to praise. Matthew 28:19-20 gives the Great Commission. Acts 13:47 quotes Isaiah 49:6. Romans 15:9-12 collects Old Testament texts on the Gentiles praising God. Revelation 7:9-10 pictures the fulfillment.
application:
Pray this psalm for your church: “Bless us so that your way may be known on earth.”

Pray for one unreached people group by name. Look up a missionary or agency your church supports.

Ask how God’s blessings to you can overflow to others.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to be gracious to you and make his face shine on you.
Ask him to let his way be known on earth.
Pray for a nation or people group to know him.
